comparisons.evidence: Q's "book-lifecycle operator for schools" can secure meaningful recurring contracts, but P combines the chain-wide "Residual-Value Exchange" with an "Outcome & Credential Lab" and "Demand-Backed Local IP Foundry," potentially transforming transaction economics, institutional revenue, and product scarcity simultaneously.

P's "Local IP Foundry" requires the chain to detect demand, acquire rights, produce content, and sell it profitably, while Q's "Institutional lifecycle operator" follows a more direct path from removing schools' sourcing, distribution, recovery, and disposal workload to recurring service fees.

P's "Outcome & Credential Lab" and "Inventory-Risk Transfer" require new educational credibility or publisher risk-sharing behaviour. Q's school lifecycle service builds more directly on existing procurement, inventory, branch, and logistics capabilities, with administrators paying for identifiable operational relief.

P specifies a two-store test with "30-, 60- and 90-day buyback quotes" and explicit stop conditions; Q similarly specifies a "100-title buyback-floor experiment" measuring conversion, returns, grading cost, resale time, and total margin. Both make their leading mechanisms readily testable.

Q's strongest reframings include "Sell publisher decisions, not shelf exposure" and guaranteed resale. P adds comparably plausible but less conventional levers such as transferring inventory risk upstream, selling verified reading outcomes, and pre-funding chain-owned intellectual property from observed local demand.

Q credibly spans institutional operations, circular resale, publisher experimentation, and literacy contracts. P covers those regions while also introducing distinct pathways through inventory-risk transfer, owned rights, publisher-funded attention, household-library management, distributed book infrastructure, and collectible authentication.

P retains attention-consuming speculative mechanisms such as "Reader Capital Pools," "Attention Escrow," and "Civic Memory Nodes" before reaching its recommendations. Q explicitly removes mechanisms judged "too peripheral, labour-intensive, or weakly connected" and concentrates its final portfolio around four mutually reinforcing businesses.
